question: State the purpose of a vulnerability assessment.

points: A vulnerability assessment systematically identifies, classifies and prioritises security weaknesses/vulnerabilities in systems, networks and applications so they can be remediated before attackers exploit them (1)

question: Explain the difference between a false positive and a false negative in vulnerability scanning.

points: A false positive occurs when a vulnerability scanner reports a vulnerability that does not actually exist â€” wasting security team time investigating non-issues (1)
A false negative occurs when a scanner fails to detect a vulnerability that does exist â€” creating a false sense of security; this is more dangerous as it leaves real vulnerabilities unaddressed (1)
Regular scanning with multiple tools, manual verification of results, and keeping scanners updated with the latest vulnerability signatures helps reduce both types of errors (1)

question: Describe the difference between black box, white box and grey box penetration testing.

points: Black box: the tester has no prior knowledge of the system â€” simulates an external attacker starting from scratch (1)
White box: the tester has full knowledge including source code, network diagrams, and credentials â€” simulates an insider threat or thorough audit (1)
Grey box: the tester has partial knowledge (e.g. a user account but no admin access) â€” simulates an attacker who has gained some level of access (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award 2 marks for any two types correctly described.

question: State what OWASP stands for and its purpose.

points: Open Web Application Security Project â€” it publishes the OWASP Top 10, a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks, used as a standard for security testing (1)

question: Explain the difference between Static Application Security Testing (SAST) and Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST).

points: SAST analyses source code, bytecode or binary code without executing the application â€” it is a 'white box' approach that finds vulnerabilities early in development (1)
DAST tests the application while it is running â€” it simulates attacks against the live application from the outside, a 'black box' approach that finds runtime vulnerabilities (1)

SAST finds issues like SQL injection in code before deployment; DAST finds issues like misconfiguration or authentication flaws that only appear when the application is running. Both are complementary â€” SAST early in SDLC, DAST on deployed/staging environments (1)

question: Describe the difference between an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS).

points: An IDS monitors network traffic and alerts administrators when suspicious activity is detected â€” it does not take action to block traffic (passive) (1)
An IPS also monitors traffic but can actively block or drop malicious traffic in real time â€” it sits inline in the network path and can prevent attacks before they reach the target (active) (1)

scenario: An IT services company manages security for multiple clients and needs to centralise security monitoring.
question: Explain the functions of a SIEM system and how it benefits security operations.

points: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects and aggregates log data from multiple sources â€” firewalls, servers, IDS/IPS, endpoints â€” into a central platform (1)
It applies correlation rules to identify patterns that indicate security incidents â€” e.g. multiple failed logins followed by successful login from an unusual location (1)
It generates real-time alerts for security teams, enabling faster detection and response to threats (reduces MTTD â€” Mean Time to Detect) (1)
SIEM dashboards provide visibility across the entire IT estate and support compliance reporting/auditing requirements (e.g. GDPR, PCI DSS log retention) (1)
Discover: identify all assets and scan them for vulnerabilities using automated tools and manual assessment (1)
Assess and Prioritise: evaluate each vulnerability's severity (CVSS score) and the risk it poses to the specific organisation â€” not all vulnerabilities are equally critical (1)
Remediate: apply patches, configuration changes or compensating controls to fix the highest-priority vulnerabilities (1)
Verify and Report: confirm the fix was effective through rescanning, document actions taken, and report on the organisation's security posture (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award 2 marks for any two phases correctly described with detail.

question: State what MTTD and MTTR stand for in security metrics.

points: MTTD: Mean Time to Detect â€” the average time taken to discover a security incident. MTTR: Mean Time to Respond/Remediate â€” the average time taken to respond to and resolve an incident once detected (1)

scenario: A financial services company must comply with PCI DSS and ISO 27001.
question: Explain the importance of regular security audits and continuous monitoring for compliance.

points: Regular audits verify that security controls are implemented correctly and consistently across all systems â€” identifying gaps before they can be exploited (1)
Continuous monitoring provides real-time visibility of the security posture â€” detecting configuration drift where systems deviate from the secure baseline (1)

Both are essential for maintaining compliance certifications (ISO 27001, PCI DSS) â€” failure to demonstrate ongoing compliance can result in fines, loss of certification, and inability to process card payments or bid for certain contracts (1)

scenario: A financial services company has hired a security firm to conduct a penetration test on their online banking platform.
question: Explain the phases of a penetration test that the security firm will follow, from start to finish.

points: Reconnaissance — gather information about the target (domain names, IP ranges, employee details from OSINT) — both passive and active (1)
Scanning and enumeration — use tools (Nmap, Nessus) to identify open ports, running services, and potential vulnerabilities (1)
Exploitation — attempt to exploit identified vulnerabilities to gain access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate test data (1)
Reporting — document all findings with risk ratings, evidence (screenshots/logs), and prioritised remediation recommendations for the client (1)

scenario: An IT services company manages security for multiple clients and needs to detect threats across all client environments.
question: Explain how a SIEM system helps detect security incidents that would be missed by manual log review.

points: SIEM aggregates logs from ALL sources (firewalls, servers, endpoints, cloud) into one platform — manual review across hundreds of systems is impossible (1)
Correlation rules connect seemingly unrelated events — e.g. 5 failed logins + successful login + large data transfer from same IP = potential breach (1)
Real-time alerting means incidents are detected in minutes rather than days or weeks — reduces MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) (1)
Centralised dashboards provide visibility across all client environments simultaneously — a single analyst can monitor multiple clients (1)

question: Describe the vulnerability management lifecycle and explain why it must be continuous.

points: Discover all assets and scan for vulnerabilities — new vulnerabilities are discovered daily, so scanning must be continuous (1)
Assess and prioritise based on CVSS severity and organisational risk — internet-facing critical vulnerabilities must be patched first (1)
Remediate (patch, reconfigure), verify (rescan to confirm), and report — the cycle repeats because new vulnerabilities are constantly discovered (1)

question: Compare SAST and DAST as application security testing approaches.

points: SAST analyses source code without executing the application (white box) — finds vulnerabilities early in development like SQL injection or buffer overflows (1)
DAST tests the running application from outside (black box) — finds runtime vulnerabilities like misconfigurations or authentication flaws (1)
SAST provides detailed code-level findings with exact line numbers but may produce false positives (1)
DAST simulates real attacks and produces fewer false positives but cannot see the code — the two are complementary and should be used together (1)
